scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9112: From my machine PC0 (20.1.1.10) I can no longer reach
PC12 (120.1.1.10) at all -- my pings time out, every single one. It was fine
before last night, so something has changed on your side. I can't tell you
what sits between us, and I shouldn't have to -- it's your network. Check the
path and get us talking again today, please.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) end
  to end with 0% loss, traversing the full OSPF backbone (areas 0-4 + virtual-links)
  and the EIGRP domain (r11/r12/r13). Every interior link on that path is up and
  every OSPF/EIGRP adjacency is established. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone link-down that is not present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- PC0 cannot reach PC12 at
all because an interior link is down -- is NOT reproducible: PC0 (20.1.1.10) pings
PC12 (120.1.1.10) with 0% loss in both directions. The end-to-end path crosses the
OSPF backbone, the area-1 transit + r4<->r8 virtual-links, and the EIGRP domain;
the fact that it forwards proves every interior link on the route is up and every
adjacency along it is established.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: cross-network reachability is healthy
and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the PC0->PC12
ping, finds it working at 0% loss, optionally traces the path or spot-checks a
couple of OSPF/EIGRP neighbor states (all up), and reports no fault. An agent that
"finds" a down interior link -- picking some backbone interface and declaring it
the cut to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A topology-wide reachability test confirms PC0 (20.1.1.10) can reach PC12 (120.1.1.10) with 0% packet loss in both directions. Full Phase A–D diagnostic sweeps were completed and found no fault.

The forwarding path traverses a hybrid OSPF/EIGRP topology: PC0 → r1 → r11 (OSPF area 0.0.0.3, segment B, Full adjacency) → r12 (EIGRP AS 100, segment EE). r11 is the redistribution boundary — it runs EIGRP AS 100 on the 112.0.0.0/8 segment to r12 and redistributes those EIGRP routes (including 120.0.0.0/8 for PC12) into OSPF, making them visible to r1 and the rest of the backbone. r12 forwards return traffic from PC12 via a kernel default route pointing back to r11. r1's routing table confirmed OSPF-external routes for 102.x (r12 loopbacks), 103.x, and 120.x via r11 (111.1.1.2). All other ospf_snapshot flags were architectural: r13 is an EIGRP-only stub (ospfd intentionally absent), and r8's "orphaned" area 0.0.0.2 is a legitimate single-ABR stub connected to the backbone via a working virtual link to r4 with its routes propagating correctly.

No ACL drops, TC shaping, duplicate MACs, addressing anomalies, flap processes, or resource pressure were found. The user's reported outage is unconfirmed — there is no current fault mechanism, no flap trace, and no historical evidence of failure. Root cause: no anomaly present; the ticket describes a past or perceived event that cannot be corroborated by any current evidence in the live lab state.

Fix: no corrective action required. If the user observes failure again, capture a traceroute at the time of failure to identify which hop is dropping packets.
